Classification of living things:
Classification is the grouping of living things by shared features. Scientists use levels from large to small: kingdom, phylum, class, order, family, genus and species. A species is a group of organisms that can reproduce and have fertile offspring. Each species has a two-part scientific name, genus first and species second, such as Panthera leo.

The main kingdoms are animals, plants, fungi, protists and bacteria. Classification helps scientists name, study and compare the huge number of living things, and it shows how closely related they are.
Features used to group animals:
Animals are grouped by body features. The first big split is vertebrates, which have a backbone, and invertebrates, which do not. Vertebrates include fish, amphibians, reptiles, birds and mammals. Other features are body symmetry, body covering (scales, feathers, fur), type of reproduction (eggs or live birth), and body temperature.

Endotherms (warm-blooded) keep a steady body temperature using their own energy. Ectotherms (cold-blooded) take their temperature mostly from the environment. Animals in the same group share several features, not just one.
Adaptation of animals to their environme:
An adaptation is a body feature or behavior that helps an animal survive and reproduce in its environment. Adaptations can be structural, such as a camel's wide feet, behavioral, such as migration or hibernation, or physiological, such as storing water in the body.

Adaptations come from natural selection: animals with helpful features survive and pass them to their young over many generations. Examples include camouflage, thick fur in cold places, and webbed feet for swimming. An animal well adapted to one habitat may not survive in a very different one.
